role.altitude: The host keeps greeting, seating, handing out menus, coordinating the floor and handling concerns; writing bookings in a paper book, typing specials and walking to check tables shrink.
skills_to_grow: Running the reservation platform's seating plan during service
role.ambitious_version: A host who spends the evening at the door with guests instead of on the phone.

tasks.short: Check menus and drinks cards, print the daily specials insert, provide guests with menus and mention specials, and collect and replace worn menus.

steps.what: Host checks that menus and drinks cards are clean and current before service
Host types and prints the daily specials insert from the chef's list today; after the change prints it from a template filled with the specials in the till
Host checks the printed insert against the chef's list: dishes, descriptions and prices
Host puts the checked specials insert into the menus
Host provides guests with menus at the table and mentions the specials
Host collects menus and replaces worn copies

approvals.approved_version: The day's specials insert with dishes, descriptions and prices exactly as checked by the host in s2c, put once into the menus for that service; any change needs a new check and a new print.

tasks.design: Handing out menus stays a greeting at the table. The only change: the specials insert is printed from a template filled with the day's specials as they stand in the till ({OTHER}), so the host no longer retypes the chef's list; the host checks the printed insert and puts it into the menus.
tasks.previous_blocker: Nothing blocked it; the work is hospitality.
tasks.enabler_now: Till systems hold the day's items and can fill a print template.
tasks.still_hard: Everything that makes guests feel welcome.
tasks.human_edge: Reading which guests want advice and which want to be left alone.
tasks.altitude: Nothing changes in the host's evening.

reach.learn: Whether specials entered in the till match what is printed.

evidence.claim: Till systems keep the day's items and prices and can fill a print template.

assumptions: Boundary: from menus ready to menus collected; taking orders is the server's work.
Input contract for s2: the day's specials with name and price entered in the till by the chef, which happens anyway so they can be sold; fallback is typing from the chef's list.
Handing out menus, checking the insert and putting it in keep their full time. s2 keeps 40 for printing and fixing the odd template line.
unknowns: Whether the restaurant prints a specials insert daily.
research_questions: Do printed specials still differ from the till?

incremental.description: No ongoing upkeep: the chef enters the specials in the till anyway, and the check of the insert is shown as s2c.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: the chef enters the specials in the till too late, so the host still types the insert and s2 keeps 100 (0.0); high: specials are in the till before the host prints (1.8).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Brief kitchen and servers on bookings with special requests, relay guest requests and concerns during service, check table status, handle complaints with the manager and note guest preferences.

steps.what: Host checks the service sheet before service: allergies, celebrations, group sizes and late bookings
Host hands the checked service sheet to the kitchen and servers
Host tells the kitchen and servers about bookings with allergies, celebrations and large groups: by reading out the book today; after the change by explaining what the service sheet shows
Host relays guest requests and concerns to servers and the kitchen during service
Host walks the floor and asks servers which tables are about to free up
Host addresses customers' concerns and complaints with the manager
Host notes guest preferences in the guest profile after the visit

approvals.approved_version: The service sheet for that service with bookings, allergies, celebrations and group sizes exactly as checked by the host in s1c, handed once to the kitchen and servers; a later booking change needs a new check or a word to the kitchen.

tasks.design: Booking notes that guests enter in the booking widget, or the host enters on phone bookings, print on a service sheet from the reservation platform ({OTHER}) ; the host checks the sheet before service and hands it to the kitchen and servers, so the briefing covers only what needs a word. Where the till is linked to the platform, a table shows as freeing up when its bill is closed, so the host walks the floor less. Relaying requests and handling concerns stay with the host.
tasks.previous_blocker: Booking notes sat in a paper book and table status only in servers' heads.
tasks.enabler_now: Reservation platforms print service sheets and can link to tills for table status.
tasks.human_edge: Turning a complaint into a guest who comes back.
tasks.altitude: A little less walking; decision rights do not change.

reach.learn: Whether closed bills reflect when tables really free up.

evidence.claim: A reservation platform offers a digital seating plan and shows the guest's profile and booking history.
Allergy notes are health data; record only what the kitchen needs for this visit, with consent.

assumptions: Boundary: contact during and around service; menu planning is outside.
Input contract for s1: booking notes entered by guests in the booking widget or by the host on phone bookings; the platform prints them on the service sheet.
Input contract for s3: bill-closed events from the till, produced when servers close a bill as they do today; about 70% of restaurants' tills can link to the platform; s3 is priced at that share.

Relaying requests, complaints, profile notes, checking and handing out the sheet keep their full time. s1 keeps 80 because reading out each booking note drops, while allergies and groups are still talked through. Booking notes come from the booking itself, so no new entry is needed.
unknowns: Whether the till links to the reservation platform.
research_questions: Do guests wait less for a table?

incremental.description: No ongoing upkeep beyond the check before service, which is shown as s1c.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: the till cannot link to the platform, so the host still walks the floor and s3 keeps 100 (3.6); high: about 70% of tills link as assumed (11.6).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Assign sections to servers, seat guests to spread the load, watch the flow of service and step in, and brief staff before service.

steps.what: Host assigns sections and tables to servers at the start of the shift
Host seats guests so that each server's load stays even
Host supervises and coordinates dining room staff during service and steps in when service slows
Host briefs staff before service on bookings, groups and specials

tasks.design: Sections per server are set on the reservation platform's seating plan ({OTHER}) instead of a paper chart, and the plan shows covers per section from bookings and the tables the host has seated, so balancing load needs less counting. Supervising service and briefing staff stay with the host.
tasks.previous_blocker: Sections and loads were tracked on paper and in the host's head.
tasks.enabler_now: Reservation platforms show seating plans with sections and covers.
tasks.human_edge: Seeing a server going under before guests notice.
tasks.altitude: Nothing much changes in the host's evening.

reach.learn: Whether covers per section match staffing.

evidence.claim: Reservation platforms provide seating plans and a central guest database.
Covers per server could be used to watch staff performance, which needs works council consent where one exists.

assumptions: Boundary: floor coordination during service; staff scheduling is outside.
Input contract for s2: covers per section from bookings in the platform and from the host's own seating taps in this step.
Covers per section are not used to rate servers.

Supervision and briefing keep their full time. s1 keeps 85 because the plan keeps last shift's sections and only changes are made, instead of redrawing the paper chart; deciding sections stays. s2 keeps 95 because the plan counts covers per section, while the host taps each seating to keep it current.
unknowns: Number of servers and sections per service.
research_questions: Do loads per server even out?

incremental.description: Host sets up sections in the plan when the room layout changes.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: sections change every shift, so nothing is saved on assigning and s1 keeps 100 (1.4); high: sections mostly carry over (3.7).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Take guests' calls about bookings, hours and directions, write phone bookings in the book, transfer calls to the manager or kitchen, and call back voicemail.

steps.what: Guests phone for bookings, opening hours, directions and menu questions
Guest books online in the widget or through the texted booking link
Host answers telephone calls and responds to inquiries about bookings, hours and the menu
Host writes phone bookings in the paper reservation book
Host transfers calls to the manager or kitchen
Host listens to voicemail and calls guests back

tasks.design: A booking widget on the website and listings lets guests book within table capacity and opening hours, and the phone line offers to text a booking link, so part of the booking calls move online. Opening hours and directions are kept current on the website and listings. Remaining phone bookings are typed straight into the reservation platform ({OTHER}) with the caller's profile on screen, replacing the paper book; transfers and call-backs stay with the host. No voice bot is used.
tasks.previous_blocker: The paper book meant every booking had to come through the phone.
tasks.enabler_now: Reservation platforms offer booking widgets, texted booking links and caller profiles.
tasks.still_hard: Regulars and older guests who prefer to call.
tasks.human_edge: A warm voice on the phone that makes guests want to come.
tasks.altitude: Fewer calls during service; decision rights do not change.

reach.learn: How many bookings move online and whether no-shows fall with reminders.

evidence.claim: A reservation platform offers a booking widget, Reserve buttons on search and social sites, a phone link that texts a booking link, and the caller's profile during a call.
A phone or chat bot must tell callers they are dealing with AI; the design uses none.

assumptions: Boundary: calls to the restaurant; group and event sales are outside.
Input contract for s2: online bookings made by guests in the widget (s1), with about the effort of a call; table capacity and hours set by the manager in the platform.
Coverage: about a third of today's calls are bookings or hours questions that move online; s2 and s5 are priced at that share.

Transfers keep their full time; guests' time is outside the host's savings, and their online booking is shown as s1o. s3 keeps 70 because a third fewer bookings come by phone; typing a phone booking into the platform takes as long as writing it in the book.
unknowns: Share of bookings by phone today.
research_questions: How many calls remain after the widget goes live?

incremental.description: Host checks online bookings with notes before service.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: regular guests keep calling and only a sixth of calls move online, so s2, s3 and s5 keep 85 (12.3); high: a third of calls move online as assumed (25.6).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional
